concepts_used: Article 358: Suspension of Article 19 during National Emergency

solution.concept_anchor: Article 358 scope — war vs armed rebellion ground
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know Article 358 suspends Article 19 often assume this happens for all three grounds of National Emergency, not realising armed rebellion is excluded.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) — Article 358 operates automatically only when Emergency is proclaimed on grounds of war or external aggression, not armed rebellion.
Eliminate (c) — Article 358 is self-executing upon proclamation; no separate Presidential Order is required, distinguishing it from Article 359.
Eliminate (d) — The 44th Amendment requires laws made during Emergency to be reasonably related to it; the blanket-cover claim is false.
Confirm (b) — Article 358 does NOT apply when National Emergency is proclaimed on grounds of armed rebellion; suspension of Article 19 is confined to war/external aggression grounds.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the assumption that Article 358 applies uniformly to all three grounds of National Emergency. Students who memorise 'Article 358 suspends Article 19 during Emergency' without noting the 44th Amendment's restriction on the ground of armed rebellion will choose (a). The key precision is that the 44th Amendment carved out armed rebellion from Article 358's automatic operation — a distinction that renders Article 19 alive even during certain Emergencies unless targeted through an Article 359 Order.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 358 grants automatic suspension of rights under Article 19 the moment a National Emergency is proclaimed, but only when the ground is war or external aggression. When the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion', it simultaneously limited Article 358's applicability to exclude this new ground. So during an Emergency on armed rebellion grounds, Article 19 is NOT automatically suspended — the government would need a specific Presidential Order under Article 359 to restrict enforcement of Article 19.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Article 358 does not apply to armed rebellion Emergency.
• Option (b): Correct — Article 358 operates only for war/external aggression grounds.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Article 358 is automatic, unlike Article 359 which requires a Presidential Order.
• Option (d): Incorrect — The 44th Amendment requires reasonable nexus between Emergency-era laws and the Emergency itself.

Value Addition:
• The 44th Amendment (1978) is the single most important reform of Emergency law — know all four changes it introduced.
• Article 358 is the only provision that actually extinguishes the right; Article 359 only suspends the remedy.
• India has never proclaimed Emergency solely on armed rebellion grounds as of 2024.

concepts_used: Article 359: Presidential Order Suspending Enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Articles 20 and 21: The Inviolable Core during National Emergency

solution.concept_anchor: Article 359 scope and exclusion of Articles 20 and 21

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, the President may issue an Order suspending the enforcement of any Fundamental Right under Part III, including Articles 20 and 21.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 expressly excludes Articles 20 and 21 from its scope — the President cannot issue an Order suspending enforcement of these two Articles even during National Emergency, a protection introduced by the 44th Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 may be limited in territorial application, covering only a part of India rather than the whole country.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 explicitly allows the President's Order to apply to the whole or any part of the territory of India, enabling geographically targeted suspension of enforcement.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, the Fundamental Rights themselves are not suspended — only the right to move any court for enforcement of the specified rights is suspended.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the critical distinction between Articles 358 and 359: Article 358 actually extinguishes Article 19 rights, while Article 359 only bars judicial enforcement — the rights continue to exist on paper.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students may believe all three statements are correct, missing that Statement 1 contains a deliberate falsehood regarding Articles 20 and 21.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — it claims Articles 20 and 21 can be included in a Presidential Order under Article 359; this is false as the 44th Amendment expressly excluded these Articles.
Evaluate Statement 2 — territorial limitation of Article 359 Orders is constitutionally permitted; this statement is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 359 suspends the remedy, not the right itself; this is the defining distinction from Article 358 and is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is not — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is crafted to trap students who know that Article 359 deals with Fundamental Rights during Emergency but are imprecise about which rights are excluded. The phrase 'any Fundamental Right under Part III' sounds authoritative and comprehensive, making it easy to mark as correct. The 44th Amendment's express exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 from Article 359's reach is a high-precision fact that separates well-prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 359 creates a Presidential Order mechanism to suspend the judicial enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights during National Emergency. Unlike Article 358 which automatically extinguishes Article 19 rights, Article 359 is discretionary and the rights survive on paper while courts cannot be approached.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) explicitly carved out Articles 20 and 21 from Article 359. No Presidential Order can suspend enforcement of these two Articles under any circumstances.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Order can be limited to specific territory — a nuanced feature allowing targeted suspension.
• Statement 3 — Correct: This is the foundational distinction — under Article 359 the right exists but is unenforceable; under Article 358 the right itself is suspended.

Value Addition:
• Parliament must lay every Article 359 Order before both Houses and can modify or revoke it.
• Once Emergency ends, all past violations of rights that were under an Article 359 Order can be challenged — unlike Article 358 violations which cannot be questioned.
• The President can also revoke an Article 359 Order before the Emergency itself ends.

concepts_used: Distinction between Suspension of Rights (Article 358) vs. Suspension of Remedies (Article 359)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 358 vs 359 — rights suspended vs remedies suspended

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 358, the State can enact laws inconsistent with Article 19 during Emergency, but such laws become void immediately upon revocation of the Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Laws enacted during Emergency under Article 358 are not automatically void upon Emergency revocation — they remain valid; it is the future application of Article 19 that resumes, not a retroactive invalidation. Laws inconsistent with Article 19 made during a valid Article 358 period cannot be challenged for Emergency-era violations.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, once the Emergency is revoked, a citizen can challenge violations of the suspended Fundamental Rights that occurred during the Emergency period.
statement_analysis.reason: Because Article 359 only suspends the remedy (court enforcement), not the right itself, once the Emergency ends and the Order is lifted, past violations of those rights become challengeable — this is the practical significance of the rights-remedy distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Articles 358 and 359 require a Presidential Order to become operative during National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 operates automatically upon proclamation of Emergency on war/external aggression grounds — no separate Presidential Order is needed. Only Article 359 requires the President to issue a distinct Order specifying the rights whose enforcement is suspended.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because Statement 2 is actually correct, and students who incorrectly mark it as 'not correct' will choose an option that includes it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — it claims Article 358 laws become void immediately upon Emergency revocation; this is incorrect since the right to challenge Emergency-era Article 358 violations does not revive.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Article 359 only suspends the remedy; once Emergency ends, past violations can be questioned. This statement is correct, not incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 358 is automatic; it does not require a Presidential Order. This statement is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct; Statement 2 is correct — the question asks which are NOT correct, so select (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the common confusion about what happens to Emergency-era legislation after the Emergency ends. Students who partially know that 'Emergency-era laws lapse' may over-apply that principle to Article 358 laws. In reality, laws enacted under Article 250 (State List) lapse six months after Emergency, but laws enacted restricting Article 19 under Article 358 are not void for Emergency-era violations. Statement 3 targets students who blur the automatic/discretionary distinction between Articles 358 and 359.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Articles 358 and 359 is one of the most high-yield conceptual comparisons in Emergency law.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Laws made under the cover of Article 358 that restrict Article 19 rights are not automatically void upon Emergency's end for the Emergency period. The right to challenge Emergency-era violations under Article 358 does not revive post-Emergency, unlike under Article 359.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Because Article 359 only suspends the remedy and not the right, once the Emergency and the Presidential Order end, citizens can challenge violations that occurred during the period.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 358 is self-executing — the moment Emergency is proclaimed on war/external aggression grounds, Article 19 stands suspended without any further Presidential action. Article 359 alone requires a separate Presidential Order.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 = Rights suspended (Article 19 extinguished for Emergency duration).
• Article 359 = Remedies suspended (rights survive but courts cannot be approached).
• The 44th Amendment added the 'reasonably related' requirement for Article 358 to prevent abuse.

concepts_used: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976): The Habeas Corpus Case
Evolution of Supreme Court's Attitude toward Emergency Powers: From ADM Jabalpur to Puttaswamy

solution.concept_anchor: ADM Jabalpur — facts, dissent, and overruling

statement_analysis.statement: In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976), the majority of the Supreme Court held that during a National Emergency under Article 359, detained persons have no locus standi to approach courts for a writ of habeas corpus.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise holding of the majority in ADM Jabalpur — that the Presidential Order under Article 359 suspended the right to approach courts, leaving detenues without judicial remedy.

statement_analysis.statement: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud authored the sole dissent in ADM Jabalpur, arguing that the right to life is rooted in natural law and cannot be taken away even by a Presidential Order.
statement_analysis.reason: The dissent was authored by Justice H.R. Khanna, not Justice Y.V. Chandrachud. Justice Chandrachud was part of the majority. Justice Khanna's dissent is considered one of the greatest in Indian judicial history.

statement_analysis.statement: The ADM Jabalpur judgment directly contributed to the enactment of the 44th Constitutional Amendment, which made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable during National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: The controversy surrounding ADM Jabalpur and the excesses of the 1975–77 Emergency were the primary motivating factors behind the 44th Amendment's protection of Articles 20 and 21 from suspension.

statement_analysis.statement: The nine-judge bench in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) unanimously held that ADM Jabalpur was incorrectly decided.
statement_analysis.reason: All nine judges in Puttaswamy concurred that ADM Jabalpur was wrongly decided, affirming that the right to life and personal liberty is inherent and cannot be suspended even by a Presidential Emergency Order.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know there was a famous dissent in ADM Jabalpur may not recall whether it was Khanna or Chandrachud, and 'Only two correct' feels like an under-count given how significant the case is.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — the majority holding on habeas corpus in ADM Jabalpur is accurately described; this is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the dissent in ADM Jabalpur was by Justice H.R. Khanna, not Justice Y.V. Chandrachud who was in the majority; this statement is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — the 44th Amendment's protection of Articles 20 and 21 is directly traceable to the Emergency abuses and the ADM Jabalpur controversy; correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Puttaswamy (2017) nine-judge bench unanimously overruled ADM Jabalpur; correct. Three out of four statements are correct — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in Statement 2 is a classic UPSC trap. Justice H.R. Khanna and Justice Y.V. Chandrachud are both towering judicial figures from the same era, and students who know 'a famous judge dissented in ADM Jabalpur' without pinning the name precisely will accept the false attribution. Justice Chandrachud's association with personal liberty jurisprudence (his grandson D.Y. Chandrachud later wrote extensively on privacy in Puttaswamy) compounds the confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976) is the most consequential — and most criticised — Supreme Court judgment on Emergency powers. The majority held that Presidential Orders under Article 359 completely ousted judicial jurisdiction, leaving detenues with no remedy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The majority ruling on habeas corpus suspension is accurately stated.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The sole dissent was by Justice H.R. Khanna, not Justice Y.V. Chandrachud. Chandrachud J. was part of the five-judge majority. Khanna J. paid a professional price for his courage — he was superseded for the Chief Justice position.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 44th Amendment was a direct legislative response to Emergency abuses, especially the ADM Jabalpur holding.
• Statement 4 — Correct: In Puttaswamy (2017), all nine judges held ADM Jabalpur incorrectly decided, making right to life inherent and inalienable.

Three statements are correct — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent is quoted in constitutional law globally as a model of judicial courage.
• Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21.
• ADM Jabalpur was decided 4-1; Khanna J. was the lone dissenter.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional Articles — National Emergency effects on legislature and finance
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly matches most pairs but swaps the Articles for 'tenure extension of State Assemblies' (172) and 'distribution of revenues' (354), exploiting the fact that both involve Presidential/Parliamentary action during Emergency.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item A — Parliament legislating on State List during Emergency is Article 250; this eliminates options that pair A with any other article.
Anchor on List I item C — Tenure extension of State Legislative Assemblies during Emergency is under Article 172 (read with Article 83); options pairing C with Article 354 are eliminated.
Anchor on List I item D — Modification of revenue distribution between Centre and States during Emergency is Article 354; confirm this eliminates options misassigning D.
The only option consistent with all four correct pairings is (c): A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap swaps Articles 354 and 172 — both operate during National Emergency and both involve Parliamentary approval, making the swap subtle. Students who have generalised memory ('some article for finances, some for tenure') without precise article numbers will attempt a plausible-sounding wrong combination. The additional confusion arises because Article 83 (tenure of Parliament) and Article 172 (tenure of State Assemblies) are close in memory, and students may erroneously apply Article 83 to state assemblies.
solution.final_explanation:
National Emergency triggers a cascade of constitutional provisions altering centre-state relations.

Correct matchings:
• A (Parliament legislates on State List) → Article 250: Parliament gains competence over State List subjects during National Emergency; laws cease effect six months after Emergency ends.
• B (Special majority for approval) → Article 352(4): Both Houses must approve by 2/3 of members present and voting plus majority of total membership within one month.
• C (Tenure extension of State Assemblies) → Article 172: Parliament — not the state legislature — extends state assembly tenure; it ceases six months after Emergency ends.
• D (Modification of revenue distribution) → Article 354: Presidential Order can alter Centre-State revenue sharing; requires Parliamentary approval and lapses after the financial year in which Emergency ends.

Trap pairing: Articles 354 (financial) and 172 (tenure) are commonly swapped because both involve Emergency-triggered modifications requiring Parliamentary sanction.

Value Addition:
• Article 250 laws lapse six months after Emergency; they do not lapse immediately.
• It is Parliament, not the President, that extends tenure under Articles 83 and 172.
• Financial Emergency (Article 360) modifies financial relations differently — Article 354 applies only during National Emergency.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment — Articles 20 and 21 made non-suspendable
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are factually correct, leading many students to hastily select (a) without examining whether R actually explains A causally.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 44th Amendment (1978) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even during National Emergency under Article 359.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Minerva Mills (1980) judgment held that Fundamental Rights are part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The 44th Amendment was enacted in 1978 before the Minerva Mills judgment (1980). The Amendment was motivated by the excesses of the 1975–77 Emergency and the ADM Jabalpur controversy — not by the Minerva Mills ruling. R is a factually correct statement about a different development that occurred two years after A.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does NOT explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits reversed-causation. Both the 44th Amendment's protection of Articles 20 and 21 and the Minerva Mills judgment are real, important, and related to Emergency jurisprudence. A student who sees 'both are true' and senses thematic connection will choose (a). But Minerva Mills (1980) came after the 44th Amendment (1978) — it could not have caused it. The actual driver of the Amendment was the 1975–77 Emergency experience and the ADM Jabalpur judgment, not Minerva Mills.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) was Parliament's legislative response to the abuses of the 1975–77 Emergency. One of its most significant provisions was making Articles 20 and 21 immune from suspension under Article 359 — no Presidential Order can bar the enforcement of these two articles.

Assertion (A): Correct — The 44th Amendment explicitly excludes Articles 20 and 21 from the President's power under Article 359.

Reason (R): Correct — Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) did hold that Fundamental Rights are part of the basic structure. This is an accurate statement of law.

Causal link: Absent. The 44th Amendment was enacted in 1978; Minerva Mills was decided in 1980. The Amendment's motivation was the ADM Jabalpur case (1976) and the experience of arbitrary detention during the Emergency — not the Minerva Mills ruling which had not yet occurred. R cannot explain A when A preceded R by two years.

Correct answer: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• ADM Jabalpur (1976) → 44th Amendment (1978) → Minerva Mills (1980): know this sequence.
• Minerva Mills held that the power to amend cannot destroy the basic structure, including Fundamental Rights.
• Articles 20 and 21 are the only two Fundamental Rights immune from both Article 358 and Article 359.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological sequence — Emergency proclamation to revocation safeguards
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) places Parliamentary approval before the Cabinet's written recommendation, which sounds procedurally logical but reverses the actual constitutional sequence of events.
elimination_logic: The process begins with the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet to the President — this must precede the Presidential Proclamation; eliminate any option placing this after the Proclamation.
After proclamation, Parliamentary approval must follow within one month with special majority — this is the second step.

If Lok Sabha is dissolved at the time of proclamation, Rajya Sabha approves first, then the reconstituted Lok Sabha must approve within 30 days of its first sitting — this is a contingent step that follows approval.

Revocation by Lok Sabha resolution (simple majority at special sitting demanded by 1/10th of members) is the final safeguard and can only logically come after continuation — correct order is D→A→C→B, confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets students who confuse the one-month window for Parliamentary approval with the 30-day window applicable when Lok Sabha is dissolved. Additionally, placing Cabinet recommendation and Presidential proclamation in the wrong sequence is a common error — students sometimes think the President can proclaim first and get Cabinet ratification later, which is incorrect under the 44th Amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment instituted a multi-step procedural safeguard for National Emergency to prevent the unilateral use of Emergency power by the Prime Minister alone.

Correct sequence:
1. (D) Written recommendation of Union Cabinet to President — The President cannot proclaim Emergency without a prior written communication from the Cabinet; this was introduced by the 44th Amendment.
2. (A) Presidential Proclamation of National Emergency — Only after receiving Cabinet recommendation.
3. (C) Parliamentary approval by special majority within one month — Both Houses must pass it by 2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership.
4. (B) Lok Sabha resolution for revocation by simple majority at a special sitting — This is the check on continuation, triggered by 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members giving notice.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a): Places Parliamentary approval before Cabinet recommendation — incorrect.
• Option (c): Places revocation mechanism before Parliamentary approval — illogical.
• Option (d): Omits the Cabinet recommendation as the first step entirely.

Value Addition:
• Before 44th Amendment, only the PM's advice was needed — Cabinet was not required to formally recommend.
• Special majority = 2/3 of members present and voting AND majority of total membership of each House.
• Revocation needs only simple majority — an asymmetry designed to make it easier to end Emergency than to continue it.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 226 not suspended during Emergency — HC writ jurisdiction survives
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students know Article 32 can be suspended and may assume this shuts down all judicial remedies, not realising Article 226 (High Court writs) remains available.
elimination_logic: Identify that a Presidential Order under Article 359 has suspended enforcement of Article 32 — this removes the Supreme Court's constitutional remedies jurisdiction for those specified rights.
Evaluate whether Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction) is also suspended — Article 226 cannot be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359; only Article 32 can be.
Eliminate (a) — The detainee cannot approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 if the Order covers Article 22; that route is blocked.
Eliminate (b) and (c) — These assume all judicial remedies are extinguished or that Article 226 is also suspended; Article 226 is not suspendable under Article 359, confirming (d) as correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a scope-extension error — students who know 'judicial enforcement of Fundamental Rights is suspended during Emergency' over-extend this to all courts. The critical distinction is that Article 359 can suspend Article 32 (Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction for FRs) but it cannot suspend Article 226 (High Courts' writ jurisdiction). This makes High Courts potentially the last available judicial forum during Emergency — a fact of enormous constitutional significance.
solution.final_explanation:
During National Emergency, a Presidential Order under Article 359 was issued suspending enforcement of Articles 22 and 32. Ramesh, detained under preventive detention without the safeguards of Article 22, wishes to seek judicial relief.

Applicable principle: Article 359 can suspend the enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights including Article 32 (right to move Supreme Court). However, Article 226 — the High Court's writ jurisdiction — cannot be suspended by any Emergency provision. It is not subject to Article 359 Orders.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Article 32 petition to the Supreme Court is barred when Article 32 is included in the Presidential Order.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Not all judicial remedies are extinguished; Article 226 survives.
• Option (c): Incorrect — A writ under Article 136 (special leave petition) to the Supreme Court for enforcing a suspended right is not available as an alternative route when Article 32 itself is suspended.
• Option (d): Correct — Ramesh can approach the High Court under Article 226. High Courts retain writ jurisdiction even when Article 32 is suspended under Article 359.

Value Addition:
• This distinction made High Courts the last refuge for detenues during the 1975–77 Emergency.
• Article 226 is broader than Article 32 — it covers not just Fundamental Rights but any legal right.
• The Supreme Court itself acknowledged in ADM Jabalpur that Article 226 was not suspended.

(b) Ramesh has no judicial remedy available since both the Supreme Court and the High Courts lose jurisdiction when an Article 359 Order is in force
(c) Ramesh can file a special leave petition before the Supreme Court under Article 136, which is not covered by the Presidential Order

solution.concept_anchor: Financial Emergency does not affect Fundamental Rights
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because 'State Emergency' (President's Rule) does remove democratic accountability, which students may loosely associate with FR restrictions, leading them to pick it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute — the question asks which Emergency type directly impacts Fundamental Rights of citizens.
National Emergency (Article 352) via Article 358/359 restricts Fundamental Rights — this qualifies.
State Emergency (Article 356) removes elected government and can enable Union executive to restrict FRs in the state — this qualifies as having FR impact.

Financial Emergency (Article 360) affects salaries, financial propriety, and directions to states — it has NO provision akin to Articles 358 or 359 and does NOT affect Fundamental Rights of citizens — this is the odd one out, confirming (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap works by making students think all three types of Emergency are similarly constitutionalised regarding Fundamental Rights. Students who loosely associate Emergency with FR suspension will group all three together. Financial Emergency's complete absence of any FR-restriction mechanism is the precise distinguishing fact that makes it the odd one out here.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests whether students can distinguish between types of Emergency on the specific parameter of Fundamental Rights impact.

• Option (a) Financial Emergency (Article 360): Correct odd one out. Article 360 contains no provision equivalent to Articles 358 or 359. It does not suspend or restrict any Fundamental Right. Its effects are limited to financial directions to states and reduction of salaries of government servants including judges.
• Option (b) National Emergency (Article 352): Directly impacts Fundamental Rights through Articles 358 (automatic suspension of Article 19) and 359 (Presidential Orders suspending enforcement of other FRs).
• Option (c) State Emergency (Article 356): While primarily affecting governance, it enables the Union executive to exercise state-level power, which can indirectly bear on civil liberties.
• Option (d) National Emergency on external aggression grounds: A sub-category of (b) that activates Article 358's automatic suspension of Article 19.

Value Addition:
• Financial Emergency has never been proclaimed in India's history.
• Article 360 requires only simple majority in Parliament — unlike National Emergency which requires special majority.
• Financial Emergency, once proclaimed, continues until revoked — no periodic renewal is needed.

Article 358: Suspension of Article 19 during National Emergency

solution.concept_anchor: Article 358 covers only Article 19 — not Articles 14 and 15

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: When a National Emergency is proclaimed on grounds of external aggression, Article 358 automatically suspends Articles 14, 15, and 19 — all rights in Part III that protect individual liberty against State action.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 suspends only Article 19 — it does not cover Articles 14 or 15. Articles 14 and 15 remain fully operative during Emergency unless specifically included in a Presidential Order under Article 359.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Articles 14 and 15 can be suspended during National Emergency only through a Presidential Order under Article 359, and not automatically through Article 358.
statement_analysis.reason: This is accurate — Articles 14 and 15 are not within Article 358's automatic scope. If the President wishes to suspend their enforcement, a specific Article 359 Order naming these Articles must be issued.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know that Emergency broadly restricts freedoms may assume all personal liberty articles including Articles 14 and 15 fall under Article 358's automatic suspension.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Article 358 explicitly covers only Article 19; Articles 14 and 15 are not mentioned in Article 358 and are not automatically suspended; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — The only way Articles 14 and 15 can have their enforcement suspended is through a specific Presidential Order under Article 359 naming those Articles; Statement 2 is correct.
One statement incorrect and one correct — select option (c): Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap makes Statement 1 appear plausible by grouping Articles 14, 15, and 19 together as 'rights protecting individual liberty against State action' — a description that is generically accurate but does not reflect the precise constitutional architecture of Article 358. Students who conceptually equate 'Emergency suspends Fundamental Rights' with 'all FRs are suspended automatically' will mark Statement 1 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
A critical precision point: Article 358 is surgically narrow — it covers only Article 19, nothing else. The right to equality (Article 14) and prohibition of discrimination (Article 15) are unaffected by Article 358's automatic operation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 358 suspends only Article 19. Articles 14 and 15 continue to be enforceable during Emergency unless specifically covered by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
• Statement 2 — Correct: This precisely captures the constitutional mechanism. A targeted Article 359 Order is the only route through which enforcement of Articles 14 and 15 can be suspended.

Value Addition:
• During the 1975–77 Emergency, no Presidential Order under Article 359 included Article 14 — courts retained jurisdiction to enforce equality rights, though they exercised extreme deference.
• Article 32 (right to constitutional remedies) can be suspended under Article 359 — this effectively guts all Fundamental Rights enforcement even if the rights themselves are not suspended.
• Article 19 has six sub-rights (19(1)(a) to (g)); all six are simultaneously suspended when Article 358 operates.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion'
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because 'civil unrest' sounds like a reasonable constitutional term and students who vaguely remember that the original wording was changed may pick a plausible-sounding phrase.
elimination_logic: The original Article 352(1) used the phrase 'internal disturbance' as the third ground for National Emergency — this is the term that was replaced.
The 44th Amendment (1978) substituted 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' to raise the threshold significantly.
Eliminate 'civil unrest' and 'public disorder' — these are not constitutional terms; eliminate 'insurrection' — though closer, it is not the precise constitutional term used.
The blank requires 'armed rebellion' — the exact term introduced by the 44th Amendment — confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets students who know that a change was made but confuse the old term ('internal disturbance') with the new one ('armed rebellion') or select a plausible-sounding but incorrect alternative like 'insurrection' or 'civil unrest'. The 44th Amendment's precise linguistic substitution is a frequently tested fact that requires exact recall.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 352(1) originally listed three grounds for National Emergency: war, external aggression, and internal disturbance. The third ground was deliberately vague, enabling its misuse in 1975.

• Option (a) 'internal disturbance': Incorrect — this was the original pre-1978 term that the 44th Amendment replaced. It is no longer the operative term.
• Option (b) 'armed rebellion': Correct — the 44th Amendment substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance', raising the threshold to require an organised, armed challenge to the State.
• Option (c) 'civil unrest': Incorrect — not a constitutional term; a plausible-sounding fabrication.
• Option (d) 'insurrection': Incorrect — though conceptually adjacent, this is not the term used in Article 352(1) as amended.

Value Addition:
• The change from 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' was directly motivated by the 1975 Emergency which was proclaimed on internal disturbance grounds.
• Article 358's automatic suspension of Article 19 does NOT apply to the armed rebellion ground — only to war and external aggression.
• India's 1975 Emergency proclamation would not have been constitutionally possible under the stricter 'armed rebellion' threshold.

solution.concept_anchor: Lok Sabha dissolution — Emergency approval by Rajya Sabha first
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because it gives the correct one-month window but applies it to the wrong body (dissolved Lok Sabha), which the student may not examine carefully.
elimination_logic: Recall the constitutional provision: if Lok Sabha is dissolved when Emergency is proclaimed, Rajya Sabha must approve within one month of proclamation.
The reconstituted Lok Sabha must then approve within 30 days of its first sitting — not one month of proclamation.
Eliminate (a) — it states the dissolved Lok Sabha must approve within one month, which is structurally impossible for a dissolved house.
Eliminate (b) and (d) — they mistate the timeline or body responsible; only (c) correctly pairs 'Rajya Sabha approves first, then new Lok Sabha within 30 days of reconstitution'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places the correct time windows (one month, 30 days) with the wrong constitutional bodies or events. Students who memorise 'one month approval window' without attaching it to the specific body (Rajya Sabha, not Lok Sabha) when Lok Sabha is dissolved will select an incorrect option. The additional nuance — 30 days from the new Lok Sabha's first sitting, not 30 days from proclamation — is the precision that separates prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 352(4) has a special provision for when the Lok Sabha is dissolved at the time of Emergency proclamation.

• Option (a): Incorrect — the dissolved Lok Sabha cannot approve anything; the approval must come from Rajya Sabha within one month.
• Option (b): Incorrect — placing the timeline as 30 days from proclamation for the reconstituted Lok Sabha is wrong; it is 30 days from the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha.
• Option (c): Correct — if Lok Sabha is dissolved, Rajya Sabha alone approves within one month. The reconstituted Lok Sabha must then approve within 30 days of its first sitting, or the Emergency ceases.
• Option (d): Incorrect — it misattributes the 30-day window to Rajya Sabha rather than the reconstituted Lok Sabha.

Value Addition:
• If the reconstituted Lok Sabha does not approve within 30 days of its first sitting, the Emergency lapses from that point.
• This provision ensures that even a freshly elected Lok Sabha with a changed mandate can check Emergency continuation.
• Rajya Sabha's role here is particularly significant since it cannot be dissolved — it provides continuity during a Lok Sabha vacancy.

solution.concept_anchor: Parliament extends State Assembly tenure during Emergency — not state legislature

statement_analysis.statement: During National Emergency, it is Parliament — and not the concerned State Legislature — that can extend the tenure of a State Legislative Assembly beyond five years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 172 provides that during National Emergency, Parliament may by law extend the tenure of a State Legislative Assembly — the state legislature itself lacks this power. This is a significant centralising feature of Emergency.

statement_analysis.statement: The extension of tenure of Lok Sabha during National Emergency can be done for a period not exceeding five years at a time.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 83(2), the extension of Lok Sabha's tenure during Emergency is limited to one year at a time, not five years. The annual renewal requirement ensures periodic parliamentary reconsideration.

statement_analysis.statement: Any extension of a State Assembly's tenure granted during National Emergency automatically ceases within six months after the Emergency ends.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an express constitutional safeguard — the extension is not permanent. Article 172 provides that tenure extension ceases six months after the Emergency ends, ensuring democratic elections are restored promptly.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students may think all three statements are correct, not catching the 'five years' error in Statement 2 which should be 'one year'.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Parliament extending state assembly tenure is expressly provided in Article 172; state legislatures lack this power. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Article 83(2) allows extension of Lok Sabha tenure one year at a time, not five years; the 'five years' qualifier makes this statement incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — the six-month post-Emergency cessation of tenure extension is a constitutional safeguard under Article 172; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap substitutes 'five years' for 'one year' — a temporal-swap within a plausible sentence about constitutional tenure. Students who know that Lok Sabha's normal tenure is five years and that Emergency allows an extension may automatically associate 'five years' with the extension period without recalling the 'one year at a time' restriction. The one-year-at-a-time rule is a critical check on indefinite Emergency continuation.
solution.final_explanation:
National Emergency creates significant distortions in the normal federal and democratic architecture, including effects on legislative tenures.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 172 gives Parliament the power to extend state assembly tenures during Emergency. The state legislature cannot extend its own life — only Parliament can do so from Delhi.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 83(2) allows Lok Sabha tenure extension only one year at a time during Emergency. The 'five years' figure is wrong. This annual renewal prevents permanent entrenchment of an Emergency-era Parliament.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Constitutional safeguard under Article 172 — the extension lapses within six months of Emergency ending, ensuring elections are held.

Value Addition:
• The same six-month post-Emergency cessation rule applies to Article 250 laws (Parliament's laws on State List).
• India extended Lok Sabha tenure during the 1962 Emergency (Chinese aggression) — this is the only historical instance.
• The one-year-at-a-time limit means Parliament must actively renew the extension every year, creating annual accountability check.

44th Constitutional Amendment (1978): Safeguards against Emergency Abuse

solution.concept_anchor: Judicial review of National Emergency — standard of review and 44th Amendment

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Constitutional Amendment, the Supreme Court can review the merits of the threat assessment made by the Union Cabinet while recommending National Emergency, including whether the threat was genuinely serious enough to warrant Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts apply a highly deferential standard of review for national security matters. Judicial review extends to examining procedure (written Cabinet communication) and mala fides — not the merits of the threat assessment. Courts do not second-guess the Cabinet's evaluation of the severity of the security threat.

statement_analysis.statement: The requirement under Article 352(5) that Emergency proclamation be based on a written communication from the Union Cabinet was introduced by the 44th Amendment, making the proclamation justiciable to a limited extent.
statement_analysis.reason: This is accurate — the 44th Amendment introduced Article 352(5) which requires the Cabinet's written recommendation, enabling courts to verify procedural compliance, thus making the proclamation partially justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: In Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court held that a National Emergency proclamation is completely non-justiciable and falls entirely within the domain of executive discretion.
statement_analysis.reason: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain and Minerva Mills established that courts can examine whether the proclamation was mala fide or based on wholly extraneous grounds. The complete non-justiciability position was rejected — courts can review at least for mala fides and procedural compliance.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) which names Statement 2 as incorrect is deceptive because Statement 2 is actually correct — students who are unsure may include it in their 'incorrect' selection.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — courts do not review the merits of the threat assessment; they examine only procedure and mala fides; this statement is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Article 352(5) written Cabinet communication requirement was indeed introduced by the 44th Amendment; this statement IS correct, not incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain did not hold Emergency completely non-justiciable; limited judicial review was affirmed; this statement is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct; Statement 2 is correct — the question asks which are NOT correct, so select (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a plausible-fabrication: it sounds like a logical extension of the 44th Amendment's transparency requirements — 'if Cabinet must give written reasons, surely courts can examine those reasons on merit?' This sounds reasonable but is constitutionally incorrect. Courts restrict themselves to procedural and mala fide review, not substantive review of the threat assessment. This trap catches students who reason from principles rather than from precise constitutional doctrine.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review of National Emergency proclamation is limited but not absent — a nuanced position established through cases like Minerva Mills and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Courts cannot review the merits of the threat — whether the threat was serious 'enough' is not for courts to decide. They review only (a) whether the Cabinet's written communication was made and (b) whether the proclamation was mala fide or colourable exercise of power.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 44th Amendment's Article 352(5) mandated written Cabinet communication, creating a reviewable procedural requirement. This is correctly stated.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Supreme Court did not hold Emergency completely non-justiciable in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain. The Court confirmed limited judicial review — mala fide proclamations can be struck down.

Value Addition:
• S.R. Bommai (1994), though directly about Article 356, reinforced that Presidential satisfaction must be based on objective material — influencing Emergency jurisprudence.
• Minerva Mills (1980) held that judicial review itself is part of the basic structure — it cannot be completely excluded even during Emergency.
• The standard for reviewing Emergency proclamations is more deferential than for Article 356 (President's Rule) because national security is involved.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 354 — Presidential Order required for revenue modification
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students correctly associate National Emergency with automatic alterations of Centre-State relations (like Article 250's legislative expansion) and erroneously extend this automaticity to financial provisions.
elimination_logic: Recall Article 354: the President can modify provisions for distribution of revenues between Centre and States during National Emergency.
Identify that this modification is NOT automatic — it requires a specific Presidential Order (Presidential Order, not automatic proclamation effect).
Eliminate (a) — the modification does not cease immediately when Emergency ends; it continues for the financial year in which Emergency ends.
Eliminate (b) and (c) — (b) claims automatic operation (incorrect); (c) confuses the mechanism with Financial Emergency. Confirm (d) as correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'automatic' for 'requires Presidential Order' — exploiting students' generalisation that Emergency automatically alters all Centre-State relations. Article 250 (legislative powers over State List) operates more directly, but Article 354 (financial modification) requires a distinct Presidential Order. This 'automatic vs. discretionary' distinction runs through multiple Emergency provisions and is a perennial UPSC testing theme.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 354 empowers the President to modify the provisions of Articles 268 to 279 relating to distribution of revenues between Centre and States during National Emergency.

• Option (a): Incorrect — the modification does not cease immediately when Emergency ends. It continues for the remainder of the financial year in which Emergency ends.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the modification under Article 354 is not automatic. Unlike Article 358 (which operates automatically), Article 354 requires the President to issue a specific Order.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Article 354 is specific to National Emergency (Article 352). Article 360 (Financial Emergency) has its own separate mechanism for financial directions.
• Option (d): Correct — Article 354's modification requires a Presidential Order and must be laid before Parliament. It lapses at the end of the financial year in which the Emergency itself ends.

Value Addition:
• Article 354 is distinct from Article 360 (Financial Emergency) — do not conflate them.
• Parliament must be notified of every Article 354 Order.
• The financial year-end rather than Emergency-end as the cessation point creates a practical buffer for budget planning.

Articles 20 and 21: The Inviolable Core during National Emergency

solution.concept_anchor: MISA, Ninth Schedule, and 44th Amendment protection of Articles 20 and 21

statement_analysis.statement: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 39th Amendment (1975) to protect it from judicial review, but this immunity was later struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980).
statement_analysis.reason: The 39th Amendment placed MISA in the Ninth Schedule specifically to prevent judicial scrutiny during the Emergency. Minerva Mills (1980) held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati date) are not immune from basic structure review.

statement_analysis.statement: Even during the 1975–77 Emergency, when MISA was extensively used for preventive detention, individuals could not be subjected to ex post facto punishment or double jeopardy, as Article 20 was not and could not be suspended.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment (enacted 1978 for future protection) confirmed what was arguably already implicit — but during 1975–77, even without the 44th Amendment's express protection, no Presidential Order under Article 359 had actually excluded Article 20 in 1975. Post-44th Amendment, this protection is absolute.

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional basis for preventive detention laws during Emergency is exclusively Article 359, which suspends all Fundamental Rights including Article 22 protections.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional basis for preventive detention laws is primarily Article 22(3) to (7), which itself allows Parliament to make preventive detention laws irrespective of Emergency. Article 359 is an additional mechanism that suspends the right to challenge such detention, but it is not the exclusive or primary basis for preventive detention law.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all three statements are correct is deceptive because Statements 1 and 2 are both correct, making it tempting to assume Statement 3 is also correct without analysing it critically.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — MISA's placement in the Ninth Schedule by the 39th Amendment and its later judicial examination in Minerva Mills is accurate; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Article 20 was not suspended during 1975–77 Emergency (no order excluded it); protection from ex post facto law and double jeopardy remained; Statement 2 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 22(3)–(7) is the primary constitutional basis for preventive detention laws; Article 359 is a supplementary mechanism to suspend the right to challenge detention, not the exclusive basis; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is not — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap. It correctly identifies that Article 359 is relevant to preventive detention during Emergency but fabricates 'exclusively' and conflates the constitutional basis for the law (Article 22) with the mechanism for suspending challenges to the law (Article 359). Students who know 'Article 359 matters for Emergency detention' may not catch the overstatement of exclusivity.
solution.final_explanation:
MISA and Emergency detention law is a historically and constitutionally rich area that tests both legal precision and historical awareness.

• Statement 1 — Correct: MISA was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 39th Amendment (1975) to immunise it from judicial scrutiny. Minerva Mills (1980) held that Ninth Schedule laws added after April 1973 can be reviewed for basic structure violations — effectively exposing MISA to scrutiny.
• Statement 2 — Correct: During 1975–77 Emergency, no Presidential Order excluded Article 20. Even if one had been issued, the 44th Amendment now makes Article 20 absolutely non-suspendable. Detenues retained protection from ex post facto punishment and double jeopardy.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliament's power to make preventive detention laws derives from Article 22(3)–(7) read with the legislative lists — this power exists even outside Emergency. Article 359 only allows suspension of the remedy to challenge such detention during Emergency.

Value Addition:
• Ninth Schedule immunity for post-April 1973 laws was finally settled in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007).
• MISA was repealed after the Emergency ended in 1977.
• Article 22 is unique — it provides procedural safeguards for ordinary arrest AND separately allows Parliament to make preventive detention laws.

concepts_used: Press Freedom and Article 19(1)(a) during National Emergency
Article 358: Suspension of Article 19 during National Emergency

solution.concept_anchor: Article 19(1)(a) press freedom suspension — grounds distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are correct and thematically related to the same Emergency, making students skip the causal analysis and assume R explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. During the 1975 Emergency proclaimed on internal disturbance grounds, pre-censorship of the press was imposed and Article 19(1)(a) was restricted.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. Article 358 does NOT apply to Emergency proclaimed on internal disturbance (now armed rebellion) grounds — it applies only to war and external aggression grounds. The 1975 Emergency suspension of Article 19 was done through a Presidential Order under Article 359, not through Article 358's automatic operation.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Select (c) — A is correct (press was censored in 1975 Emergency) but R is incorrect (Article 358 did not apply to the 1975 internal disturbance Emergency).
solution.final_explanation:
The 1975 Emergency is the most instructive episode for understanding how Emergency provisions interact with press freedom.

Assertion (A): Correct — During the 1975 Emergency, pre-censorship of newspapers was imposed. Editors left columns blank in protest. The press was effectively muzzled during this period.

Reason (R): Incorrect — This is the critical precision point. The 1975 Emergency was proclaimed on grounds of 'internal disturbance' (now 'armed rebellion' post-44th Amendment). Article 358's automatic suspension of Article 19 applies only when Emergency is on grounds of war or external aggression — NOT internal disturbance. The restriction on press freedom during 1975 was effected through a Presidential Order under Article 359, not through Article 358's automatic operation. R incorrectly attributes the suspension mechanism.

Correct answer: (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The 1975 Emergency was the only Emergency proclaimed on internal disturbance grounds — the other two (1962 and 1971) were on external aggression grounds where Article 358 did apply.
• Post-Emergency, laws restricting Article 19 rights enacted during an Article 358 Emergency become unenforceable for future violations but the Emergency-period violations cannot be challenged.
• Freedom of press is not separately enumerated — it is implied in Article 19(1)(a)'s freedom of speech and expression.

Reason (R): This was because Article 358 of the Constitution, which automatically suspends Article 19 rights upon the proclamation of National Emergency, came into operation immediately upon the 1975 Emergency proclamation and remained in force throughout its duration.

Financial Emergency (Article 360) vs. National Emergency: Impact on Fundamental Rights

solution.concept_anchor: Financial Emergency — no FR impact; other Emergency effects compared

statement_analysis.statement: When National Emergency (Article 352) and State Emergency (Article 356) operate simultaneously, Parliament can legislate on both Union and State List subjects.
statement_analysis.reason: Under National Emergency, Article 250 gives Parliament power over State List. Under State Emergency, Parliament takes over the legislative function of the state legislature — together this creates complete parliamentary dominance over all legislative subjects.

statement_analysis.statement: Financial Emergency (Article 360) can suspend Fundamental Rights under Part III if the President includes them in the Emergency proclamation.
statement_analysis.reason: Financial Emergency has no mechanism to suspend or restrict Fundamental Rights — there is no equivalent of Articles 358 or 359 for Article 360. The Financial Emergency proclamation cannot include any FR suspension provision; that power does not exist under Article 360.

statement_analysis.statement: During a Financial Emergency, the President can direct that all money bills and financial bills passed by State Legislatures be reserved for Presidential consideration.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 360(3) explicitly provides that the President may give direction to states to reserve all money bills and financial bills for his consideration during Financial Emergency — this is one of the specific powers available under Article 360.

statement_analysis.statement: Financial Emergency, unlike National Emergency, does not require periodic renewal by Parliament every six months to remain in force.
statement_analysis.reason: Financial Emergency remains in force until revoked — there is no requirement of six-monthly Parliamentary renewal. This contrasts with National Emergency which must be renewed by special majority every six months.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is deceptive because three statements are indeed correct, but the student must correctly identify that Statement 2 is false — students who are unsure about Financial Emergency's FR impact may count all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — simultaneous National and State Emergency giving Parliament power over both lists is constitutionally accurate; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Financial Emergency has no FR suspension mechanism; Article 360 contains no equivalent of Articles 358/359; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 360(3) reservation of money bills for Presidential consideration is a specific Financial Emergency power; correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Financial Emergency continues until revoked with no periodic renewal requirement, unlike National Emergency; correct. Three statements correct — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 makes Financial Emergency appear to have FR-suspension capabilities by adding the plausible qualifier 'if the President includes them in the Emergency proclamation' — mimicking the structure of Article 359 Orders. Students who know Articles 358/359 work through Presidential Orders may apply that template to Article 360, not realising it has no such power.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding what each Emergency type can and cannot do with Fundamental Rights is a high-value distinction for UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Simultaneous National + State Emergency = complete legislative centralisation. Parliament legislates on all subjects.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Financial Emergency has no power to suspend or restrict any Fundamental Right. Article 360 is entirely about financial propriety and fiscal directions. No Presidential Order under Article 360 can touch Fundamental Rights.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 360(3) allows the President to reserve state money bills for Presidential assent during Financial Emergency — a significant central oversight power.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Financial Emergency continues indefinitely until revoked. National Emergency requires six-monthly Parliamentary renewal by special majority — a major structural difference.

Three statements are correct — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Financial Emergency proclamation requires only Parliament's simple majority approval — a lower bar than National Emergency.
• No Financial Emergency has ever been proclaimed in India.
• Under Financial Emergency, even judges' salaries can be reduced — Article 360(4)(b).

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment — all four key changes introduced

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for National Emergency and required the President to act on the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet.
statement_analysis.reason: Both these changes were introduced by the 44th Amendment — the substitution of 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance' in Article 352(1) and the requirement of written Cabinet communication under Article 352(5) are accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment introduced a provision enabling the President to revoke a National Emergency on his own initiative, without requiring any resolution by either House of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The President's power to revoke Emergency on his own initiative is not a 44th Amendment introduction — it existed in the original Constitution. What the 44th Amendment introduced was the new mechanism enabling Lok Sabha to compel revocation through a simple majority resolution at a special sitting demanded by 1/10th of total members.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Constitutional Amendment made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable under Article 359, but did not change anything about Article 358's scope of automatic suspension.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a partial-truth: the 44th Amendment did make Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable under Article 359, but it also affected Article 358 by adding the 'reasonably related' requirement — laws and executive actions during Emergency must have a nexus with the Emergency. This is a significant addition to Article 358 that the statement ignores.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) naming only Statement 2 as incorrect is deceptive because Statement 3 is also incorrect (it omits the 44th Amendment's effect on Article 358), making students who catch only one error choose (a) instead of the correct (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — both the 'armed rebellion' substitution and the written Cabinet recommendation requirement are accurate 44th Amendment changes; Statement 1 is correct, not incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the President's power to unilaterally revoke predates the 44th Amendment; the new addition was the Lok Sabha compulsory revocation mechanism; Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 3 — the 44th Amendment also modified Article 358 by adding the 'reasonably related' nexus requirement; Statement 3's claim that 'nothing about Article 358's scope changed' is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select (d): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap: it correctly captures one aspect of the 44th Amendment (Article 359's exclusion of Articles 20 and 21) but incorrectly asserts that Article 358 was untouched. The 44th Amendment's 'reasonably related' addition to Article 358 is a frequently overlooked reform. Students who know the 44th Amendment primarily through the Articles 20/21 protection and the Cabinet recommendation requirement miss this third change entirely.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) introduced four major safeguards against Emergency abuse. Identifying which changes it actually made — and distinguishing them from what existed before — is a precision-testing exercise.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Both the 'armed rebellion' substitution (Article 352(1)) and the written Cabinet recommendation (Article 352(5)) are genuine 44th Amendment changes.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: Presidential self-initiated revocation existed before 1978. The 44th Amendment's new addition was enabling Lok Sabha to force revocation through a simple majority resolution at a special sitting, triggered by 1/10th of members.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The 44th Amendment also modified Article 358 by adding the requirement that laws enacted and executive actions taken during Emergency must be 'reasonably related' to the Emergency — preventing use of Emergency as cover for unrelated legislation.

Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — answer is (d).

Value Addition:
• The four key 44th Amendment changes: (1) armed rebellion replaces internal disturbance; (2) written Cabinet recommendation required; (3) Articles 20 and 21 made non-suspendable; (4) Lok Sabha simple majority revocation mechanism added.
• The 'reasonably related' nexus requirement under Article 358 is the 44th Amendment's most understated reform.
• The special sitting for revocation requires notice from 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members — not 1/10th of members present.

Judicial Review of National Emergency Proclamation

solution.concept_anchor: Emergency jurisprudence timeline — ADM Jabalpur to Puttaswamy
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Minerva Mills before the 44th Amendment, which sounds plausible because Minerva Mills challenged the 42nd Amendment (not the 44th) — students may confuse the amendment numbers and reverse the sequence.
elimination_logic: Anchor: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla was decided in 1976 during the Emergency — this is the earliest event and must come first.
The 44th Constitutional Amendment was enacted in 1978 — a direct response to the Emergency abuses exposed by ADM Jabalpur; it follows ADM Jabalpur.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India was decided in 1980 — after the 44th Amendment was enacted; it challenged provisions of the 42nd Amendment.

Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India was decided in 2017 — the most recent, unanimously overruling ADM Jabalpur. Correct sequence: ADM Jabalpur (1976) → 44th Amendment (1978) → Minerva Mills (1980) → Puttaswamy (2017) = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap conflates the 42nd and 44th Amendments. Minerva Mills (1980) primarily challenged the 42nd Amendment (1976) which had sought to immunise constitutional amendments from judicial review. Students who know 'Minerva Mills struck down an Emergency-era Amendment' may place it before the 44th Amendment (1978) — which is incorrect. The 44th Amendment (1978) came after the Emergency ended and after ADM Jabalpur; Minerva Mills (1980) came later still.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of Emergency jurisprudence spans four landmark events across four decades. Knowing their sequence is essential for UPSC.

Correct sequence:
1. ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976): Supreme Court majority capitulated to Emergency, holding habeas corpus suspended. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented alone.
2. 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978): Janata government's legislative response — made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable, introduced Cabinet written recommendation, changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion', and added Lok Sabha revocation mechanism.
3. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Court reasserted basic structure doctrine, struck down key provisions of the 42nd Amendment (1976), and held Fundamental Rights are part of basic structure.
4. Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017): Nine-judge bench unanimously declared ADM Jabalpur incorrectly decided; right to life and privacy are inherent.

Why wrong options fail: Option (a) reverses 44th Amendment and Minerva Mills. Option (c) places Minerva Mills before the 44th Amendment — incorrect. Option (d) misplaces ADM Jabalpur.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills challenged the 42nd Amendment (1976), not the 44th Amendment (1978) — crucial distinction.
• The 42nd Amendment was the Emergency-era amendment; the 44th was the corrective post-Emergency amendment.
• All four events are individually UPSC-worthy — know the year of each.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 32 suspendable — Article 226 not suspendable under Article 359

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) can be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359 during National Emergency, effectively removing the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights covered by the Order.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 expressly allows the President to suspend the right to move any court (including the Supreme Court under Article 32) for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights. Article 32 can be included in such an Order, subject to the exclusion of Articles 20 and 21.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Article 226, which grants High Courts the power to issue writs, is also suspended during National Emergency when a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspends the enforcement of Article 32.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 226 cannot be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359. The suspension of Article 32 does not carry over to Article 226. High Courts retain their writ jurisdiction even when Article 32 is suspended — making them the last judicial refuge during Emergency.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who correctly know Statement 1 is true may assume both statements dealing with judicial remedies during Emergency are simultaneously correct, conflating the Supreme Court and High Court jurisdiction.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359; the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to enforce specified FRs is removed by such an Order; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction) cannot be suspended by an Article 359 Presidential Order; it is not within the scope of Article 359; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates by making Statement 2 appear to be a natural consequence of Statement 1. Students who think 'if Supreme Court jurisdiction is removed, surely High Court's is too' follow an intuitive but constitutionally wrong logic. The Constitution deliberately preserved Article 226 from Emergency suspension — a structural choice ensuring that at least one court remained accessible to citizens even during the most extreme Emergency.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Article 32 and Article 226 during Emergency is one of the most practically significant constitutional nuances.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 32 is a Fundamental Right itself (right to approach the Supreme Court for FR enforcement). Since it is a Fundamental Right under Part III, it can be suspended under a Presidential Order issued under Article 359, subject to Articles 20 and 21 being excluded. During the 1975–77 Emergency, Article 32 was indeed suspended by Presidential Order.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 226 is NOT a Fundamental Right — it is a constitutional power of High Courts. It falls outside Part III and therefore outside the scope of Article 359 Orders. High Courts retained their writ jurisdiction during the 1975–77 Emergency, though they exercised extreme restraint in practice.

Value Addition:
• Article 226 is wider than Article 32 — it covers enforcement of any legal right, not just Fundamental Rights.
• During 1975–77, High Courts were the bodies that some courts used to grant habeas corpus — this is why the government sought to amend Article 226 as well (though unsuccessfully).
• In ADM Jabalpur, the question was partly about whether High Court habeas corpus orders survived after Article 32 was suspended — further evidence of this distinction's practical importance.

solution.concept_anchor: Historical Emergency proclamations — grounds used in 1962, 1971, 1975
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know the 1975 Emergency was controversial and declared by Indira Gandhi may associate it with 'external aggression' from their vague memory of the Bangladesh war (1971), confusing the two Emergencies.
elimination_logic: The 1962 Emergency was proclaimed on grounds of external aggression — Chinese incursion in the north-eastern frontier; this is the first Emergency.
The 1971 Emergency was proclaimed on grounds of external aggression — Pakistani military action leading to the Bangladesh Liberation War.

The 1975 Emergency, the blank in the question, was proclaimed on grounds of 'internal disturbance' — the most controversial ground, used against domestic political opposition; this rules out external aggression options.
Confirm (d) — the 1975 Emergency was proclaimed on grounds of internal disturbance; neither war nor external aggression applies.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap exploits the proximity of the 1971 Emergency (external aggression — Bangladesh war, genuinely linked to external military conflict) and the 1975 Emergency (internal disturbance — entirely domestic political crisis). Students who blur these two events may fill the blank with 'external aggression' applying the Bangladesh war context incorrectly to 1975. The 1975 Emergency had no external military context — it was declared by PM Indira Gandhi citing internal political threats.
solution.final_explanation:
India has seen three National Emergency proclamations — each on different grounds.

• Option (a) war: Incorrect — no Emergency has been proclaimed on grounds of war (defined as formally declared war).
• Option (b) external aggression: Incorrect — 1975 Emergency had no external military dimension. External aggression was the ground for 1962 (Chinese aggression) and 1971 (Pakistani aggression leading to Bangladesh Liberation).
• Option (c) armed rebellion: Incorrect — 'armed rebellion' as a constitutional term did not even exist in 1975; it was introduced by the 44th Amendment (1978) to replace 'internal disturbance'.
• Option (d) internal disturbance: Correct — The 1975 Emergency was proclaimed on grounds of internal disturbance (the original pre-44th Amendment term). This was the most controversial proclamation because the 'threat' was a domestic political challenge, not an armed or external security situation.

Value Addition:
• 1962 Emergency was never formally revoked — it was allowed to lapse.
• The 1971 Emergency (external aggression) and 1975 Emergency (internal disturbance) overlapped for some months, making it the only period of concurrent Emergencies on different grounds.
• Post-44th Amendment, the 1975 type of proclamation would require evidence of 'armed rebellion' — a much higher threshold.

solution.concept_anchor: Emergency provisions — Articles 358, 359, FR suspension mapping
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because it correctly matches several pairs but conflates Articles 14 and 19 — placing Article 14 under Article 358's automatic suspension scope, which is incorrect.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item A — 'Automatically suspended during Emergency on war/external aggression grounds without Presidential Order': This describes Article 19 under Article 358; A must match with 3 (Article 19).
Anchor on List I item B — 'Non-suspendable under Article 359 — expressly excluded': This describes Articles 20 and 21; B matches 4.

Anchor on List I item C — 'Can be suspended only through a specific Presidential Order under Article 359': This describes Articles other than 19, 20, and 21 — including Article 22 and Article 14; C matches 2 (Article 22).

List I item D — 'Not covered by Article 358; remains enforceable unless specifically included in an Article 359 Order': This precisely describes Articles 14 and 15; D matches 1. Correct: A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges Article 14 (right to equality) with Article 19 (six freedoms) in students' minds under the general label 'Emergency suspends fundamental freedoms'. Students who think Article 358 suspends all major Fundamental Rights — rather than only Article 19 — will incorrectly match Article 14 under Article 358's automatic scope (List I item A), producing the wrong combination. The correct position is that Article 14 is entirely outside Article 358 and requires a specific Article 359 Order.
solution.final_explanation:
This matching exercise maps specific Fundamental Rights to their Emergency-period constitutional treatment.

Correct matchings:
• A (Automatically suspended without Presidential Order during war/external aggression Emergency) → Article 19: Article 358 operates automatically for Article 19 upon proclamation on war/external aggression grounds.
• B (Non-suspendable — expressly excluded from Article 359) → Articles 20 and 21: The 44th Amendment made these two Articles absolutely immune from any Presidential Order under Article 359.
• C (Can be suspended only through specific Presidential Order under Article 359) → Article 22: Article 22 (protections against arbitrary arrest) can be included in a Presidential Order — and was during the 1975 Emergency.
• D (Not covered by Article 358; remains enforceable unless included in an Article 359 Order) → Articles 14 and 15: The right to equality and non-discrimination — not within Article 358's automatic scope, can only be restricted through Article 359 Order.

Trap pairing: Articles 19 and 14 are the most commonly conflated pair here.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 covers only Article 19; Article 359 can cover any FR except Articles 20 and 21.
• During 1975 Emergency, Article 359 Orders suspended Articles 14, 19, 21, and 22 — though post-44th Amendment, Article 21 cannot be suspended.
• Article 32 (right to approach SC) can also be suspended under Article 359.
